summary:
Project HRYAH is a browser game that puts you on a space agency's mission team. Every launch runs through three phases: design a spacecraft under mass, power, delta-v, data and budget limits; fly it to orbit from a zero-g station where crises and docking mistakes can damage it; then operate it in orbit, switching camera, transmitter, heater and safe mode through sunlight, eclipse, ground-station passes and solar storms.

After each launch, a causal debrief traces the outcome back to the exact decisions behind it (for example, power lost on the first orbit, traced to a small battery paired with a solar array with camera it could not support). Money, research and lessons carry into the next launch window of a multi-launch campaign, played solo or with friends online. Scenarios range from a first CubeSat and flood response to lunar and Mars mapping, an Apophis-style asteroid flyby and station resupply, each tied to a real space mission.

The physics (Tsiolkovsky, Kepler, eclipse geometry, the Rayleigh limit) and component values are checked against NASA's Small Spacecraft Technology report. Systems engineering is hard to teach because every subsystem affects every other one. HRYAH lets players fail, see exactly why, redesign and fly again: the loop real mission teams use.
details:
What it does

Project HRYAH turns the life of a small-satellite mission into a short, replayable game loop. A campaign is a series of launch windows, and every launch goes through three phases.

1. Design. Players pick an engine, solar panels, a battery, an antenna and a payload (a camera, or a cargo container for resupply missions), then a launch vehicle, propellant load and target altitude. A live check panel shows the coupled margins: delta-v to reach the orbit, energy to get through eclipse, downlink capacity against the data the camera produces, ground resolution from aperture and altitude, the launcher's mass limit, and the budget. Change one module and the other margins move with it.

2. Flight. The launch is played inside a zero-g space station. The astronaut moves with WASD, works the consoles and handles crises and mini-games: solar-panel orientation, life support and docking. Mistakes cost delta-v or damage subsystems, and that damage follows the spacecraft into orbit. A lost spacecraft goes straight to the debrief.

3. Orbit operations. Players run the satellite one orbit at a time. Before each orbit they set the camera, transmitter, heater and safe mode while reading a forecast of sunlight, imaging windows, ground-station passes, eclipse and solar storms. Every choice trades data collection against battery charge, onboard buffer space and cold stress.

Debrief and campaign. Every failure is recorded together with the chain of causes leading back to a design or operations decision, and the debrief shows that chain in plain language. The payout depends on how much useful data reached the ground and how sharp it is, and data loses value as time passes. Between launch windows the world changes: better modules appear on the market and get cheaper, and events such as technology breakthroughs, supply disruptions, lifted sanctions or grants shift the situation. Four fictional agencies differ in budget, launcher access and industrial strengths. They can buy modules off the shelf or develop their own, with a defect risk that depends on their industry and on the module's NASA Technology Readiness Level. An agency that skips a window gives up launch income and gains research points instead.

Three ways to play. Solo campaign against three rival agencies run by the computer; hot-seat, where several players take turns on one screen; and online, where one player creates a room and shares its code so friends can join from their own devices. In every mode the agencies compete for the same science programme in the same launch windows.

Scenarios. Twelve scenarios built on ten missions, each inspired by a real mission that the game names in its briefing: NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative, Landsat 9, flood mapping by Sentinel-1, ICESat-2, Hubble's mirror flaw, OSIRIS-APEX and asteroid Apophis (2029), the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Cygnus and Dragon resupply to the ISS, cargo pre-positioning from NASA's Mars Design Reference Architecture, the James Webb Space Telescope, and today's commercial Earth-imaging constellations.

How it works

  • Deterministic simulation core. The rules are pure TypeScript functions, separate from the interface. Each phase follows one contract (init, step, isDone, finish) over plain JSON state; time arrives as an action and randomness comes from a seeded generator. The same inputs always give the same result, so runs are reproducible, and in online rooms the server replays a player's orbit commands to verify the reported result.
  • Physics. Tsiolkovsky's equation for delta-v and propellant; Kepler's third law for orbital periods; a cylindrical Earth-shadow model for eclipse duration; the Rayleigh criterion (1.22λh/D at 550 nm) for ground resolution; power and data budgets integrated over each part of every orbit. The baseline mission's delta-v requirement was checked against Hohmann transfers (vis-viva).
  • Data. Component ranges were compared with NASA's State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report (power, propulsion and communications chapters), Planet SkySat data from NASA's CSDA program, NASA Near Earth Network DVB-S2 test results and L3Harris SpaceView camera specifications. We keep a written audit that compares every game value with the published range. Where we simplified for playability, for example to make the differences between modules easy to read, the gap is documented rather than hidden.
  • Quality. More than 580 automated tests, including fuzz tests and a sweep over thousands of spacecraft designs used for balancing.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It teaches why engineers make trade-offs, not just which formula to use: the coupling between subsystems is visible during design and proven during operations.
  • Failure becomes feedback. Instead of "Game Over", players see which bottleneck failed (power, downlink, buffer, thermal, delta-v) and why, and the next launch window lets them act on it.
  • Short sessions: the CubeSat tutorial and short campaigns are designed to fit a classroom period or a club meeting, and online rooms let a whole group play together. Each scenario links the game to a real mission, so curious players have somewhere to go next.
  • Missions, modules and agencies live in data files, so new scenarios (sample return, on-orbit servicing, more planetary missions) can be added without changing the engine.

What makes it creative

  • The causal debrief: the game explains its own outcomes.
  • Information windows between phases ("Why real missions do this") connect every game step to the reason real mission teams do the same thing.
  • Spacecraft engineering, hands-on flight inside a station, and mission operations in one loop, where each phase inherits the consequences of the one before.
  • A light layer of space policy: agencies with different industries, and sanctions that force home-grown development and the defect risk that comes with it.
  • Real events as scenarios, from Hubble's flawed mirror to the Apophis flyby in April 2029.

Factors we considered

  • Realism against playability: real equations and real data ranges, simplified only where it keeps the choices readable, and documented where we did.
  • Session length: a short first campaign and quicker follow-up launches.
  • Accessibility: runs in any modern browser with nothing to install, has a CubeSat tutorial scenario, and needs no prior knowledge.
  • A team of six working in parallel: fixed contracts between phases, code review on every pull request and continuous integration.
  • Licensing: only original art or openly licensed assets, all credited.

Tools, languages and software

TypeScript, React and Vite; Three.js for the 3D spacecraft view in the design phase; Canvas 2D for the flight station; a Node.js room server for online play; Vitest for testing; GitHub and GitHub Actions for CI/CD; self-hosting on a Raspberry Pi with Caddy. Concept art and artwork were drawn in Ibis Paint and prepared as SVG. Open-source icons are credited in the resources section. AI assistance is described in the SI section.

Source code: https://github.com/Hryah/hryah (the physics audit is in docs/PHYSICS.md; the development log is in docs/DEVLOG.md).

About the name: HRYAH is our team's name. It came with us from our previous hackathon, and it is named after a cat.
